quotes.t: I myself know nothing, except just a little, enough to extract an argument from another man who is wise and to receive it fairly.

Has a philosopher like you failed to discover that our country is more to be valued and higher and holier far than mother or father or any ancestor, and more to be regarded in the eyes of the gods and of men of understanding?
The being of all virtues, and chiefly of temperance, depends on the practice of them.
There is no greater evil one can suffer than to hate reasonable discourse.

Something you want badly enough can always be gained. No matter how fierce the enemy, how remote the beautiful lady, or how carefully guarded the treasure, there is always a means to the goal for the earnest seeker.
Because monks come from the midst of purity, they consider as good and pure what does not arouse desire among other people.
Buddhas and Ancestors continuously maintain ocean mudra samadhi. While swimming in this samadhi, they expound, realize, practice.
In the great way of going beyond, no endeavor is complete without being one with myriad things. This is ocean mudra samadhi.
How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live.
That man is the richest whose pleasures are the cheapest.
Any man more right than his neighbors constitutes a majority of one.
Most of the luxuries, and many of the so-called comforts of life, are not only not indispensable, but positive hindrances to the elevation of mankind.
The world of today has achieved much, but for all its declared love for humanity, it has based itself far more on hatred and violence than on the virtues that make one human.
It is dangerous and harmful to be guided in our life's course by hatreds and aversions, for they are wasteful of energy and limit and twist the mind and prevent it from perceiving truth.
In times of crisis it is not unnatural for those who are involved in it deeply to regard calm objectivity in others as irrational, short-sighted, negative, unreal or even unmanly.
It is impossible to conceive of many without one.
The wisdom which knows what are and are not dangers is opposed to the ignorance of them.
Remember our words, then, and whatever is your aim let virtue be the condition of the attainment of your aim, and know that without this all possessions and pursuits are dishonourable and evil.
One always speaks badly when one has nothing to say.
The public is a ferocious beast: one must chain it up or flee from it.
Paradise on earth is where I am.
In love of home, the love of country has its rise.
If there were no bad people, there would be no good lawyers.

I have known a vast quantity of nonsense talked about bad men not looking you in the face. Don't trust that conventional idea. Dishonesty will stare honesty out of countenance, any day in the week, if there is anything to be got by it.
God is sitting here, looking into my very soul to see if I think right thoughts. Yet I am not afraid, for I try to be right and good; and He knows every one of my struggles.
A little Madness in the Spring Is wholesome even for the King.
I never saw a Moor, I never saw the Sea; Yet know I how the Heather looks, And what a Wave must be.
If all printers were determined not to print anything till they were sure it would offend nobody, there would be very little printed.
Ambition has its disappointments to sour us, but never the good fortune to satisfy us.
Freedom of speech is a principal pillar of a free government; when this support is taken away, the constitution of a free society is dissolved, and tyranny is erected on its ruins.
quotes.source: On Freedom of Speech and the Press

quotes.t: Nonviolence is a powerful and just weapon. Indeed, it is a weapon unique in history, which cuts without wounding and ennobles the man who wields it.
quotes.source: The Quest for Peace and Justice, 1964

quotes.t: Human progress never rolls in on wheels of inevitability; it comes through the tireless efforts of men willing to be co-workers with God, and without this hard work, time itself becomes an ally of the forces of social stagnation.
There comes a time when one must take a position that is neither safe, nor politic, nor popular but he must take it because conscience tells him it is right.
I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.
Give a girl an education, and introduce her properly into the world, and ten to one but she has the means of settling well, without further expense to anybody.
We do not look in great cities for our best morality.
In the name of God, stop a moment, cease your work, look around you.
One of the first conditions of happiness is that the link between man and nature shall not be severed.

The most difficult subjects can be explained to the most slow-witted man if he has not formed any idea of them already; but the simplest thing cannot be made clear to the most intelligent man if he is firmly persuaded that he knows already, without a shadow of doubt, what is laid before him.
quotes.source: The Kingdom of God Is Within You

quotes.t: I've found that there is always some beauty left — in nature, sunshine, freedom, in yourself; these can all help you.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: It's really a wonder that I haven't dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out.
I'm afraid that people who know me as I usually am will discover I have another side, a better and finer side.
Be nice to the whites, they need you to rediscover their humanity.
We were made to enjoy music, to enjoy beautiful sunsets, to enjoy looking at the billows of the sea and to be thrilled with a rose that is bedecked with dew.
It is through weakness and vulnerability that most of us learn empathy and compassion and discover our soul.
What I cannot love, I overlook. Is that real friendship?
When we blindly adopt a religion, a political system, a literary dogma, we become automatons. We cease to grow.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 4

quotes.t: The final lesson a writer learns is that everything can nourish the writer. The dictionary, a new word, a voyage, an encounter, a talk on the street, a book, a phrase learned.
The fear of death is more to be dreaded than death itself.
It is only the ignorant who despise education.
We desire nothing so much as what we ought not to have.
Make yourself an honest man, and then you may be sure there is one less rascal in the world.
Not what I have, but what I do, is my kingdom.
The merit of originality is not novelty; it is sincerity.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History

quotes.t: Books are the mirrors of the soul.
For books continue each other, in spite of our habit of judging them separately.
Each had his past shut in him like the leaves of a book known to him by heart
I ardently desired the acquisition of knowledge.
I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.
There is something at work in my soul, which I do not understand.
O for a Life of Sensations rather than of Thoughts!
Quality is more important than quantity. One home run is much better than two doubles.
Political tyranny is nothing compared to social tyranny and a reformer who defies society is a much more courageous man than a politician who defies Government.
To ask the 'right' question is far more important than to receive the answer.
The love we give away is the only love we keep.

I know no safe depository of the ultimate powers of the society but the people themselves; and if we think them not enlightened enough to exercise their control with a wholesome discretion, the remedy is not to take it from them, but to inform their discretion by education.
I always felt that the great high privilege, relief and comfort of friendship was that one had to explain nothing.
If you want to be loved, be lovable.
The human heart has hidden treasures, in secret kept, in silence sealed; the thoughts, the hopes, the dreams, the pleasures, whose charms were broken if revealed.
Knowledge unfits a child to be a slave.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

quotes.t: To have great poets, there must be great audiences too.
We are slaves of the law in order that we may be free.
There is an alchemy in sorrow. It can be transmuted into wisdom, which, if it does not bring joy, can yet bring happiness.
The mind is a superb instrument if used rightly. Used wrongly, however, it becomes very destructive.
In two or three hundred years life on earth will be unimaginably beautiful, marvellous.
Leading an undefeated life is eternal victory. Not being defeated, never giving up, is actually a greater victory than winning.
I never thought of losing, but now that it's happened, the only thing is to do it right. That's my obligation to all the people who believe in me. We all have to take defeats in life.
quotes.source: Statement after losing to Ken Norton, 1973

quotes.t: Lack of direction, not lack of time, is the problem. We all have twenty-four hour days.
For words, like Nature, half reveal and half conceal the Soul within.
Restlessness is discontent — and discontent is the first necessity of progress. Show me a thoroughly satisfied man — and I will show you a failure.
quotes.source: The Diary and Sundry Observations of Thomas Alva Edison

quotes.t: You cannot change your destination overnight, but you can change your direction overnight.
All my life through, the new sights of Nature made me rejoice like a child.
Risk comes from not knowing what you're doing.
If I'm honest, I have to tell you I still read fairy tales and I like them best of all.
You'll never find a rainbow if you're looking down.
Making with their rhythms something torn and new.
He who serves a revolution plows in the sea.
quotes.source: Letter to General Juan José Flores, 9 November 1830

quotes.t: There were no temples or shrines among us save those of nature.
There was a house made of dawn. It was made of pollen and of rain, and the land was very old and everlasting.
Sorrow eats time. Be patient. Time eats sorrow.
Those who are dead have never gone.
Sacred time is always in the Present.
Every soul has a distinct song.
We in Africa have no more need of being 'converted' to socialism than we have of being 'taught' democracy. Both are rooted in our past — in the traditional society which produced us.
I failed on to the next thing, until I found something.
I am not a liberator. Liberators do not exist. The people liberate themselves.
It's clear that there is no peace without justice. There is no peace without truth.

We hold that all countries, big or small, rich or poor, should be equal, and that international economic affairs should be jointly managed by all the countries of the world instead of being monopolized by the one or two superpowers.
quotes.source: Speech at the Special Session of the UN General Assembly, 1974

quotes.t: Having it isn't as good as not having it.
The glories and obstacles of the past are just a speck compared to the vastness of the future.
quotes.source: Thirty Years of Making Magic Out of Ordinariness

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Birago Diop.bio: Birago Diop was a Senegalese poet and storyteller who retold Wolof folktales in Tales of Amadou Koumba and celebrated Africa's oral tradition in poems such as 'Breaths'.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charles Eastman.bio: Dakota (Santee Sioux) physician and writer, known by his Dakota name Ohiyesa. Books such as The Soul of the Indian interpreted Native spirituality, silence and values for a wide readership in the early twentieth century.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Che Guevara.bio: Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician and writer whose journeys across Latin America, recorded in The Motorcycle Diaries, shaped his convictions. A major figure of the Cuban Revolution, his essays and speeches remain widely read and debated.

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Deng Xiaoping.bio: Deng Xiaoping was the Chinese leader who opened China to market reforms after 1978, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. His pragmatism is summed up in his saying that it does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

Jim Ryun.bio: Jim Ryun is an American former athlete who in 1964 became the first high school student to run a mile in under four minutes. He won a silver medal in the 1500 metres at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics and later served as a US Representative from Kansas.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Joy Harjo.bio: Muscogee (Creek) poet, musician and author who served three terms as United States Poet Laureate, the first Native American to hold the post. Poems such as Remember call readers back to sky, earth and ancestry.

Julius Nyerere.bio: Julius Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence in 1961 and became the first president of Tanzania. Known as Mwalimu, 'the teacher', he championed education, equality and African socialism.

Kamau Brathwaite.bio: Barbadian poet and historian whose idea of 'nation language' reshaped Caribbean poetry. He argued its rhythms should follow the hurricane and the calypso rather than the English pentameter, and he chronicled African retentions in Caribbean culture.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leslie Marmon Silko.bio: Laguna Pueblo novelist and storyteller whose Ceremony (1977) is a central work of Native American literature. Her writing weaves story, land, memory and healing into a single fabric, in the Pueblo oral tradition.

Liu Cixin.bio: Liu Cixin is a Chinese science-fiction writer, author of the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy that begins with The Three-Body Problem. He is the first Asian writer to win the Hugo Award for Best Novel.

Louise Erdrich.bio: Turtle Mountain Chippewa novelist and poet, author of Love Medicine and The Painted Drum. Her interwoven novels chronicle Ojibwe families, land and survival across generations in the northern plains.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

N. Scott Momaday.bio: Kiowa novelist, poet and essayist who won the Pulitzer Prize for House Made of Dawn in 1969, a landmark that launched the Native American Renaissance. His essays in The Man Made of Words explore language, story and identity.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Qian Zhongshu.bio: Qian Zhongshu was a Chinese scholar and novelist best known for Fortress Besieged (1947), a witty satire of intellectuals in wartime China and one of the great Chinese novels of the twentieth century.

Rigoberta Menchú.bio: K'iche' Maya activist from Guatemala who in 1992 became the first Indigenous person to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Her testimony I, Rigoberta Menchú brought the struggles of Guatemala's Indigenous peoples to world attention.

Simón Bolívar.bio: Venezuelan military and political leader who led the independence of much of Spanish South America from Spanish rule. His Angostura Address and Jamaica Letter remain foundational texts of Latin American republican thought.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
